title: Route errors without losing their status
goal: Distinguish standard output, standard error and descriptor-order effects while retaining a failing command’s actual status.
challenge: Produce separate data/error records and a combined record from the supplied failing producer. Demonstrate why reversing descriptor order routes error output differently. Retain status7 and explain the difference; do not hide failure.

steps.command: w=$(mktemp -d "$HOME/textarchive-streams.XXXXXX") && cd "$w" && saved_umask=$(umask) && umask 077 && pwd && here() { case "$w" in "$HOME"/textarchive-streams.??????) ;; *) return 19;; esac; test "${w%/*}" = "$HOME" && test -d "$w" && test ! -L "$w" && test "$(realpath -e "$w")" = "$w" && test "$(stat -c %U:%a "$w")" = learner:700 && test "$(pwd -P)" = "$w"; }; dir_ok() { test -d "$1" && test ! -L "$1" && test "$(realpath -e -- "$1")" = "$w/$1"; }; fresh() { for f; do test ! -e "$f" && test ! -L "$f" || return 19; done; }; here && test "$(df --output=avail -k . | tail -1)" -gt 65536
steps.explanation: Create and record a new private guest workspace. Stop on any failed guard; the free-space check is an observation, not a guaranteed reserve. Do not use the host terminal.
steps.expected: A unique learner-owned mode0700 directory; no originals overwritten.

steps.command:
here && fresh out.txt err.txt status.txt && { bash -c 'printf "data
"; printf "problem
" >&2; exit 7' > out.txt 2> err.txt; rc=$?; printf '%s
' "$rc" > status.txt; test "$rc" = 7; } && cat out.txt err.txt status.txt
steps.explanation: Redirections route bytes; they do not turn failure into success. Save $? before another command replaces it.
steps.expected: data, problem, and status7 in separate files.

steps.command: here && fresh combined.txt && { bash -c 'printf "data\n"; printf "problem\n" >&2; exit 7' > combined.txt 2>&1; rc=$?; test "$rc" = 7; } && cat combined.txt
steps.explanation: 2>&1 duplicates the stdout descriptor at this moment. Both streams now reach the same file.
steps.expected: Two ordered lines: data then problem.

steps.command: here && fresh only-data.txt earlier-stdout.txt && { bash -c 'printf "data\n"; printf "problem\n" >&2; exit 7' 2>&1 > only-data.txt; rc=$?; test "$rc" = 7; } > earlier-stdout.txt && cat only-data.txt earlier-stdout.txt
steps.explanation: When 2>&1 occurs first it still refers to the enclosing group’s stdout, not the subsequently opened file. This is real descriptor ordering, not transactional redirection.
steps.expected: only-data contains data; earlier-stdout contains problem.

hints: Follow which descriptor 2 duplicates before descriptor1 changes.
